name: Change in an accounting policy
definition: A change in accounting policy is a change to the accounting principle, or to the method of applying it, for a class of event or transaction that already occurred and has not changed in substance. It may be made only if required by statute, or for compliance with an accounting standard, or if it would result in a more appropriate presentation. A change with a material effect — in the current period or reasonably expected in later periods — must be disclosed, together with the amount by which each affected item changed, or the fact that the amount is not ascertainable.
why_it_exists: Consistency is a fundamental assumption, so a break in it destroys comparability across periods unless it is declared. This concept is the boundary marker for a bookkeeping system: an adjustment classified as a policy change carries a disclosure obligation, and one wrongly classified as a policy change imposes an obligation that does not exist.

adopting a policy for events or transactions that differ in substance from previously occurring ones is NOT a change in accounting policy
adopting a new policy for events or transactions that did not occur previously, or were immaterial, is NOT a change in accounting policy
common_mistakes: classifying a revised estimate as a policy change — AS 5 paragraph 22 sends the ambiguous case the other way, to estimate
treating the first-ever policy for a genuinely new kind of transaction as a change, when AS 5 paragraph 31(b) says it is not
disclosing that a policy changed but omitting the amount by which affected items changed, where that amount is ascertainable
changing a policy because it is preferred, rather than because statute, a standard, or a more appropriate presentation requires it

validation_checks: the reason recorded for the change is statute, compliance with an accounting standard, or more appropriate presentation — nothing else
the events or transactions do not differ in substance from previously occurring ones, and did occur previously and were not immaterial
if the effect is material in the current period, the amount by which each affected item changed is disclosed, or the fact that it is not ascertainable is indicated
if the effect is immaterial now but reasonably expected to be material later, the fact of the change is disclosed in the period of adoption
if the change follows adoption of an Accounting Standard, that standard's transitional provisions were applied
examples: adopting a different principle because an Accounting Standard now requires it — a change in accounting policy, accounted for under that standard's transitional provisions
counterexamples: an employer introducing a formal retirement gratuity scheme in place of ad hoc ex-gratia payments — AS 5 paragraph 31(a) states this is NOT a change in accounting policy, because the events differ in substance

evidence.quote: A change in accounting policy consequent upon the adoption of an Accounting Standard should be accounted for in accordance with the specific transitional provisions, if any, contained in that Accounting Standard.

Any change in an accounting policy which has a material effect should be disclosed. The amount by which any item in the financial statements is affected by such change should also be disclosed to the extent ascertainable. Where such amount is not ascertainable, wholly or in part, the fact should be indicated.

If a change is made in the accounting policies which has no material effect on the financial statements for the current period but which is reasonably expected to have a material effect in later periods, the fact of such change should be appropriately disclosed in the period in which the change is adopted.
Any change in the accounting policies which has a material effect in the current period or which is reasonably expected to have a material effect in later periods should be disclosed.
